scope.understood_as: Suppose the Moon simply stopped existing, now, with Earth as it is today: what would change for the oceans, for living things, for the planet's spin and its tilt, in what order, and how sure science can be of each step.
scope.boundary: It stops being this concept when the Moon is destroyed rather than gone (debris, rings, impacts), when Earth never had a Moon (a different four-billion-year history with a different spin), or when the subject becomes the real Moon slowly drifting away. A speculative disaster told as a prediction would also break it, because the premise asks what follows, not what frightens.

subject.audience_value: A 'what if' audience comes for logically developed consequences: a premise taken seriously and followed, one step at a time, to effects they would not have guessed, with the reasoning visible. For a general YouTube audience the reward is the chain itself (the next tide, the next full Moon, the night, then the deep planetary change) and knowing which links are solid and which are still argued. There are no processed references for this exercise, so this is read from the niche and from how the popular versions of this exact question are told: they lean on catastrophe and disagree with each other on the numbers, while the studies point to quieter, stranger effects.

candidates.subject: What if the Moon disappeared: the consequences in the order they would arrive
candidates.angle: Keep the premise whole and follow it outward in time, from the next tide to a million years later, saying at each step how sure science is. The honest chain is quieter and stranger than the overnight catastrophe the question usually gets.
candidates.what_happens: The Moon is gone and the viewer follows what changes, one clock at a time. The tide shrinks to the Sun's share and settles into a fixed daily rhythm. Reefs lose the full Moon that times their spawning (one coral kept under unchanging moonlight has already lost its timing in an experiment). Every night becomes a new-moon night for the animals that read moonlight. The tidal brake on Earth's spin weakens. Over a million years the tilt that sets the seasons begins to wander, and how far it would go is still disputed by the scientists who modelled it.
candidates.why_it_matters: It shows what the Moon does for Earth right now, which few viewers have thought about: it is less a light for the night than a timekeeper for the sea, for living calendars and for the planet's own axis.
candidates.reward: A chain of consequences that keeps overturning expectations (the tides don't stop, the tide stops drifting, the experiment has already been done), ending on an honest open question and a new picture of the Moon as Earth's metronome.

strongest_material.what: The premise: the Moon is gone in an instant (its mass, its pull and its light), and the Sun, Earth and planets are otherwise unchanged. Physically it cannot happen.
strongest_material.framed_as: Said once, plainly, as the rule of the game at the start ('it can't happen, so let's suppose it'), so every later step reads as reasoning from a supposition and never as a prediction.

strongest_material.what: The Sun's tide-generating force is about half the Moon's (a little less than half): the Sun is some 27 million times more massive but about 390 times farther away.
The tides would not stop. They would shrink to the Sun's share alone: on most coasts a much smaller rise and fall.
strongest_material.reasoning: With the Moon removed (the premise), the Sun's tidal force is the only one left, about half the Moon's. Today's tide is the two forces added together at full and new Moon and partly cancelling at the quarters, so what remains is a fraction of today's range: by the forces alone, roughly a third of a spring tide. Each coast's shape changes the size of its own tide, so no single local figure is claimed.

strongest_material.what: Spring tides come at full and new Moon, when Earth, Sun and Moon line up; neap tides come around the quarter Moons, when Sun and Moon pull at right angles.
Because the Moon moves along its orbit, a point on Earth needs about 50 minutes more than a day to turn back under it.
With only the Sun's tide, the sea would rise and fall by nearly the same amount every day, with no spring or neap tides, and reach high water at about the same hour every day.
strongest_material.reasoning: The spring-neap swing exists only because two tides line up and drift apart (M4); with one tide left there is nothing to line up. High water comes later each day because the Moon needs its extra ~50 minutes (M5). The Sun returns to the same place in the sky every 24 hours (that is what a solar day is), so a tide raised by the Sun alone keeps the same clock time. Small seasonal differences in the Sun's tide remain, hence 'nearly' and 'about'.

strongest_material.what: Hundreds of species of corals and other invertebrates spawn at the same time several nights after the full Moon.
In an experiment, colonies of one coral (Pocillopora damicornis) kept under constant full-moon or constant new-moon conditions released their larvae out of synchrony.
In one marine midge (Clunio marinus), moonlight sets the monthly timing in southern populations, while northern populations use water turbulence instead.
How animals sense and keep lunar time is still poorly understood; whether they carry internal lunar-month clocks is an open question.
Whether moon-timed animals would re-time themselves to another cue, and how fast, cannot be known from the evidence.
strongest_material.framed_as: Said as a question the film cannot answer: first what their clocks are known to use (including the second cue some already have), then plainly that nobody knows how they would cope.

strongest_material.what: Night animals behave differently with moonlight: eagle owls call more often, from higher perches, on moonlit nights; coyotes howl more on new-moon nights; migrating land birds set off more often as moonlight decreases.
Without the Moon every night would be as dark as a new-moon night, so behaviour tied to moonlit nights would lose its trigger, and behaviour tied to dark nights would have its conditions every night.
strongest_material.reasoning: Under the premise the only change to the night sky is the missing Moon, and at new Moon the Moon is already absent from the night sky. The animals in M12 already behave differently on such nights, so a sky that is always moonless means their dark-night behaviour every night. What that does to them over generations is the open question of M11.

strongest_material.what: Tidal friction has slowed Earth's spin: geological records give a spin about 1.22 times faster than today's 2.5 billion years ago, a day of roughly 20 hours.
With the Moon gone, the only brake left on Earth's spin would be the Sun's weaker tide, so the day would keep lengthening, but more slowly.
strongest_material.reasoning: The tides are what slowed the spin (M14), and the Moon raises the larger share of them (M2). Removing the Moon removes most of the force behind the slowing; the Sun's smaller tide keeps a weaker brake on. How much more slowly is not calculated here and is not claimed.

strongest_material.what: Today the Moon keeps Earth's tilt stable; without it the tilt would vary chaotically.
With the Moon, Earth's tilt varies only about 1.3 degrees either side of 23.3 degrees.
In one calculation with the Moon removed and Earth otherwise as it is today, the tilt swung between 15 and 32 degrees within a million years.
Milankovitch theory links the ice ages to changes in sunlight at northern latitudes caused by changes in Earth's orbit and orientation, the tilt included.
A tilt wandering between 15 and 32 degrees would make seasons noticeably milder at the low end and harsher at the high end, and would shift the sunlight pattern the ice-age rhythm follows.
strongest_material.reasoning: The tilt is what makes the seasons: the more the axis leans, the bigger the swing between summer and winter sunlight at a given latitude. Compared with today's narrow range (M17), the calculated range (M18) covers much gentler and much harsher seasons, and a change of tilt changes the northern sunlight that Milankovitch theory links to the ice ages (M19). How strongly the climate would respond is not claimed.

strongest_material.what: How far and how fast a moonless Earth's tilt would wander in the long run: the 1993 study finds very large chaotic swings (beyond 50 degrees within a few million years and past 85 in the long term, for faster early spins), while later work finds the change much slower.
strongest_material.hedge: Each figure is said with its study and its conditions, and the narration says plainly that the scientists who modelled it still disagree about the long run; no single range is given as the answer.

strongest_material.what: The Moon's loss would arrive as rhythms fading on separate clocks (the tide's within a day, life's calendar within a month, the spin's and the tilt's over ages), not as one night of catastrophe.
strongest_material.reasoning: Each consequence follows from something the Moon supplies all the time: the larger share of the tide (M2), a monthly rhythm of light that living things read (M8), and the steadying pull on the tilt (M16). Take away what keeps a rhythm and the rhythm changes, each at its own pace: the tide at its next turn, a reef at its next spawning, the axis over a million years. Nothing in this chain needs a sudden event.

progression.adds: the rule of the game and the quiet first night: the Moon is gone, nothing crashes, the night is darker and there will be no more eclipses
the next morning's tide: the sea still rises, but only by the Sun's pull, about half the Moon's, so the rise and fall shrinks
the tide becomes a plain clock: no more spring and neap tides, and high water at the same hour every day instead of about 50 minutes later
the first full Moon that never comes: reefs that spawn several nights after it, and the experiment that already took the Moon's rhythm away from one coral, whose larvae fell out of step
would life find another clock: some midges already set their month by the churn of the water, but how lunar clocks work is still poorly understood, so the honest answer is that nobody knows
every night a new-moon night: owls that call under a bright Moon, coyotes that howl more on dark nights, birds that leave on moonless nights
the brake on the planet's spin: tides have stretched the day since it lasted about 20 hours; without the Moon's share the day lengthens more slowly

the slowest change is the largest: the Moon holds the tilt near 23 degrees; without it, one calculation has the tilt wandering between 15 and 32 degrees within a million years, and the seasons with it
how far in the long run is still argued: almost anywhere given enough time, or far more slowly, depending on the study
the payoff: the Moon's real job was keeping time, and its loss arrives as rhythms fading on separate clocks, not as one catastrophe

runtime.why: Ten steps, each resting on its own material and each opening the next: the tide's rhythm sets up the creatures that read it, their nights lead to the planet's own clocks, the tilt leads to the dispute, and the dispute leads to the ending. At roughly a minute a step this fills ten minutes without repeating itself. The density suits a general what-if audience that wants one new consequence at a time with the reasoning shown, and every step has its own picture, so none needs padding.

candidates.feasibility: Illustrated stills carry it well: painted coasts and tide marks, drawn tide charts and clock faces, a night reef spawning, a lab tank beside a calendar, owls and coyotes under dark skies, a globe with a drawn fan of axis positions, timelines across scales. No footage is needed and no person has to appear. Nothing graphic, religious or superstitious is needed: the Moon's folklore, festival calendars and disaster imagery are left out. Narration and a quiet music bed are enough.

candidates.subject: Would Earth's seasons go wild without the Moon?
candidates.angle: Make the whole film the scientific argument over the Moon as the steadier of Earth's tilt, from the 1993 'climate regulator' result to the later studies that find the drift far slower.
candidates.what_happens: The film explains how the Moon's pull holds steady the tilt that makes the seasons, shows what one calculation gives when the Moon is taken from today's Earth, then follows the disagreement: a 1993 study in which a moonless tilt can drift almost anywhere given time, and a later analysis finding the drift slow enough not to threaten habitability.
candidates.why_it_matters: The tilt is the largest consequence the premise could have, reaching the whole planet's climate, and it is genuinely unsettled, so the viewer watches researchers reason about something nobody can test.
candidates.reward: Understanding why a few degrees of lean change seasons and ice ages, and why careful experts reach different answers, in place of a confident catastrophe.

strongest_material.what: Today the Moon keeps Earth's tilt stable; without it the tilt would vary chaotically.
Remove the Moon from today's Earth and one calculation has the tilt swinging between 15 and 32 degrees within a million years.
The long-run range and speed of the wandering are disputed between the 1993 study and later work.
strongest_material.hedge: Every figure is given with its study and conditions, and the dispute is said to be open.

strongest_material.what: Milankovitch theory links the ice ages to tilt-driven changes in northern sunlight.

progression.adds: how the Moon's pull holds the tilt that makes the seasons, and how small today's wobble is
what one calculation shows when the Moon is taken from today's Earth: 15 to 32 degrees within a million years
why a few degrees matter: the ice ages follow changes in tilt-driven sunlight
the argument: almost-anywhere drift for faster early spins against later findings of a much slower drift

runtime.why: Four solid steps, read in primary form, make perhaps five or six minutes for a general audience. The rest of ten minutes would have to come from history and comparisons not researched here, or from showing the same globe again.
runtime.shortfall: The history that could carry ten minutes (Ward's 1982 estimate, Mars' own wandering tilt as a living example, the 'rare Earth' argument) was not researched. Without it the material is one mechanism and one disagreement, and every consequence lies a million years away.

candidates.feasibility: Diagrams can carry it (a globe and its fan of axis positions, strips of seasons, long timelines), but with few concrete scenes it risks becoming a lecture over the same globe.

candidates.subject: The creatures that keep time by the Moon
candidates.angle: Answer the question through the living things that set their calendars by the Moon (spawning reefs, shore midges, night birds and hunters) and ask what each would do without it.
candidates.value_form: natural timekeepers and the loss of their cue
candidates.what_happens: Reef corals that spawn together a few nights after the full Moon; a coral experiment in which unchanging moonlight scattered the larvae's timing; a gene in corals more active on full-moon nights; midges that read the Moon in the south and the water's churn in the north; owls, coyotes and migrating birds whose nights change with moonlight.
candidates.why_it_matters: It shows that moonlight is information animals act on, a calendar written in light, which most viewers have never considered.
candidates.reward: A gallery of surprising natural timekeepers, and the strange thought of each one waking into a month that no longer turns.

strongest_material.what: Hundreds of coral species spawn together several nights after the full Moon.
One coral kept under constant moonlight conditions released its larvae out of synchrony.
A light-sensing gene in corals is more active on full-moon nights, which the review says suggests a role in timing spawning.
A marine midge times its month by moonlight in the south and by water turbulence in the north.
Eagle owls, coyotes and migrating land birds change their behaviour with moonlight.
How animals keep lunar time is still poorly understood.

progression.adds: reefs that spawn together a few nights after the full Moon
the coral experiment: unchanging moonlight, larvae out of step
a hint of how corals read the Moon: a light-sensing gene more active at full Moon
midges with two kinds of monthly clock, depending on the coast
owls, coyotes and night migrants that read moonlight
how little is known about how any of them keep lunar time

runtime.why: The examples are many, but each lands on the same consequence (the animal loses its cue) and the same honest ending (nobody knows whether it would re-time itself), so ten minutes would repeat one beat with different species. Everything here comes from one review read through, plus snippets.
runtime.shortfall: A second development beyond 'it loses its cue' is missing: how fast such clocks can re-time, or what would replace the Moon for them, is exactly what the review says is not understood. The dung beetle that steers by moonlight was seen only in search summaries.

candidates.feasibility: The most picturable of the four: night reefs, shores, owls, coyotes and birds make strong painted stills. Care is needed to keep every animal healthy and alive in the frame and to leave out the review's distressing examples.

candidates.subject: The Moon's slow goodbye
candidates.angle: Answer the question through the real Moon, which is slowly drifting away, as a slow-motion version of the vanishing: what its retreat has already done to Earth's day and will one day do to the tilt.
candidates.value_form: a real slow process as a stand-in for the premise
candidates.what_happens: The tides the Moon raises have been braking Earth's spin since a day lasted about 20 hours. The same slow tidal evolution, the 1993 study notes, will in the end carry Earth into the zone where its tilt turns chaotic. The Moon's measured retreat (seen here only in search summaries) would tie the two together.
candidates.why_it_matters: It grounds the hypothetical in something measurable that is happening now, so the vanishing becomes a fast-forward of a real process.
candidates.reward: The unsettling thought that the Moon is very slowly leaving already, and what that has cost the length of the day.

strongest_material.what: Geological records give a spin about 1.22 times faster than today's 2.5 billion years ago, slowed by tidal dissipation.
With the Moon the tilt stays steady until tidal dissipation in the end drives Earth into the large chaotic zone.
The Earth-Moon pair's slow tidal evolution is a slow-motion version of the vanishing: the day lengthens and, in the far future, the tilt's steadiness ends.
strongest_material.reasoning: The same tidal dissipation that lengthened the day (M33) is what the 1993 study says will eventually push Earth's tilt into chaos (M34), so the real process slowly delivers two consequences of the premise.

progression.adds: the tides have braked Earth's spin since a day lasted about 20 hours
the same slow process will one day end the tilt's steadiness
so the real Moon is acting out a very slow version of the vanishing

runtime.why: Its read material is two statements in one paper. Its central measurement, the Moon's yearly retreat, was seen only in search summaries, and most of its timeline lies billions of years ahead, where few concrete scenes exist.
runtime.shortfall: The recession measurement and its history (the reflectors left on the Moon, the laser ranging) would have to be read, and even then the angle answers a different question from the user's.

candidates.feasibility: Stills could show the reflectors, laser beams and ancient shorter days as diagrams, but the far-future half has little to picture beyond timelines.

selection.why: T1 is the only angle that answers the user's question at every scale a viewer can feel. The tide on the very next morning (the Sun's pull is about half the Moon's, confirmed by NOAA and NASA), the monthly calendar of the reefs, the nights, the day's own length, and at the end the tilt, which two independent studies agree the Moon steadies today. The research also gives it an honest shape the popular versions miss: the consequences come on separate clocks, the first ones are changes of rhythm rather than disaster, and the largest one is still argued over by the people who modelled it. The famous '0 to 85 degrees' turns out to describe faster early spins; for today's Earth the 1993 paper itself reports 15 to 32 degrees within a million years. It was close with T2, whose research is the deepest (a primary paper read in full), but T2 is T1's final movement stretched to fill a whole film. The coral experiment is T1's strongest single moment, but the choice does not rest on it, since it is one study known through one review.

over_alternatives.why_not: The tilt argument is the strongest open question in the research, but alone it asks one diagram to hold ten minutes. Its consequences unfold over a million years, the read material is three papers about chaotic spin dynamics, and the history that could carry it (Ward's 1982 estimate, Mars' wandering axis, the 'rare Earth' argument) was not researched. Inside T1 it becomes the slow, contested last movement, which lands harder after the fast consequences.

The moon-timed animals are the most picturable material, but every example ends the same way, an animal losing its cue, followed by the same honest 'nobody knows how it would adapt', so the film would repeat one beat with different species. It also drops the physical answers for the planet itself (tide, spin, tilt). Its two best cases, the spawning reefs and the coral experiment, become T1's key moment.

It answers a neighbouring question rather than the user's: a Moon retreating a few centimetres a year is not a Moon that has vanished, so it would swap the premise for the real trend. Its central measurement was seen only in search summaries, and most of its timeline lies billions of years away. Its one read fact, that tides have slowed Earth's spin since the day lasted about 20 hours, joins T1 as the brake beat.

selection.how_scope_kept: Every candidate answers the user's own question about the consequences of a vanished Moon. T1 keeps the premise whole (the Moon gone, everything else unchanged) and develops it from the first night to a million years later, never swapping in a Moon that explodes, one that never existed, or the real Moon slowly receding; T4, the one angle that would have swapped the premise, was set aside for that reason.

value_to_carry.what: The rule of the game: the Moon is simply gone, its pull and its light, with nothing else changed; it cannot happen, and the film says so.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: Every later step follows from this one rule; saying it plainly keeps the film honest and lets the viewer check the logic as it goes.
value_to_carry.framed_as: Said as a supposition at the very start ('it can't happen; suppose it did'), so every consequence reads as reasoning, not prophecy.

value_to_carry.what: The tides would not stop: the Sun raises its own tide, a little less than half the Moon's, so the sea keeps rising and falling, on most coasts much less.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It overturns the first thing most viewers expect and shows the film will reason rather than dramatise.

value_to_carry.what: The tide becomes a plain clock: nearly the same size every day, no spring or neap tides, and high water at about the same hour every day instead of about 50 minutes later.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It reveals that the Moon gives the sea a rhythm, not only a height, and sets up the idea that living things read that rhythm.

value_to_carry.what: Life keeps a calendar by the Moon, and taking away the Moon's rhythm has already been tried on one coral: hundreds of reef species spawn together several nights after the full Moon, and colonies of one coral kept under unchanging moonlight released their larvae out of step.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It turns the thought experiment into an observed result for one animal: the strongest evidence the film has that the loss would be felt by living things.

value_to_carry.what: Whether moon-timed life would find another clock is unknown: northern populations of one midge already use the water's turbulence instead of moonlight, but how animals keep lunar time is still poorly understood.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It keeps the film from claiming doom or extinction while leaving the viewer a real question to hold.
value_to_carry.framed_as: Said as an open question: what their clocks are known to use, then plainly that nobody knows how they would cope.

value_to_carry.what: Every night would be a new-moon night: owls that call more under a bright Moon, coyotes that howl more on dark nights and birds that set off on moonless nights would live for good in the dark half of their month.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It brings the consequence to the night the viewer knows and shows that moonlight is information for animals, not decoration.

value_to_carry.what: The brake on Earth's spin would weaken: tides have stretched the day since it lasted about 20 hours, 2.5 billion years ago; the Moon raises the larger share of the tides, so without it the day would lengthen more slowly.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It shows the day itself is one of the Moon's clocks and moves the film from life's calendar to the planet's.

value_to_carry.what: The slowest change is the largest: today the Moon holds Earth's tilt near 23.3 degrees, within about 1.3 either side; without it, in one calculation, the tilt swings between 15 and 32 degrees within a million years, and the seasons and the ice-age rhythm change with it.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: The tilt makes the seasons, so this is where losing the Moon would reshape the climate of the whole planet, on the planet's own time scale.

value_to_carry.what: How far the tilt would wander in the long run is argued: the 1993 study finds a moonless Earth's tilt can drift almost anywhere given enough time (for faster early spins), while later work finds the drift far slower.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It is the film's honest open question: it shows the difference between a calculation and a certainty, and gives the viewer the real range instead of the confident catastrophe this question usually gets.
value_to_carry.hedge: Each figure is said with its study and conditions, and the narration says plainly that the scientists who modelled it still disagree about the long run.

value_to_carry.what: The Moon's real job is keeping time: losing it would show up as rhythms fading on separate clocks (the tide's within a day, life's within a month, the planet's over ages), not as one night of catastrophe.
value_to_carry.why_it_matters: It answers the opening question with a new idea of the Moon the viewer can carry away, and turns the quiet first night into the start of everything that followed.
